meta.titre: Transition Elements: Electrons, Complexes and Colour

sections.contenu_markdown: An iron roofing sheet in Bamenda turns orange-brown with rust, a copper pot made by craftsmen in Foumban slowly turns green, and farmers in the Centre Region spray cocoa trees with a blue copper compound to fight black pod disease. The colours and the behaviour of all these metals come from one feature: a partly filled d subshell. Examiners at the GCE Advanced Level return to the d-block almost every year, asking about electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, complex ions, colour and catalysis. This lesson gives you the reasoning behind each of those questions.

items: Electrons fill subshells in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and one orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
Hund's rule: electrons occupy the orbitals of a subshell singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing takes place.
A dative covalent bond is a bond in which both shared electrons are supplied by the same atom.
The oxidation number of a simple ion equals its charge, and the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to zero.

sections.titre: Transition elements: definition, configurations, properties and complex ions

variantes.nom: Complex ions: ligands, coordination number and oxidation number
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must count dative bonds, find the oxidation number of the metal or write a ligand exchange equation.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A **ligand** is a molecule or ion with at least one lone pair that it donates to the central metal ion. A **monodentate** ligand forms one dative bond ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{CN^-}$), a **bidentate** ligand forms two (ethane-1,2-diamine, the oxalate ion $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$) and EDTA$^{4-}$ is hexadentate.

The **coordination number** is the number of dative bonds to the central ion, not the number of ligands. Six gives an octahedral shape, four a tetrahedral or square planar shape and two a linear shape, as in $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+$.

The **oxidation number of the metal** is the overall charge minus the sum of the ligand charges. In $[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-}$: $x + 6(-1) = -4$, so $x = +2$.

Ligand exchange changes the colour:

$$[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+} + 4\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2}]^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$$

blue to deep blue, and

$$[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+} + 4\mathrm{Cl^-} \rightarrow [\mathrm{CuCl_4}]^{2-} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}$$

blue to yellow-green (the coordination number falls from 6 to 4 because chloride ions are larger).

variantes.nom: Colours of ions and reactions with sodium hydroxide
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to identify an aqueous transition metal ion from its colour or its hydroxide precipitate.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Aqueous ion | Colour |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ | blue |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ | pale green |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ | yellow-brown |
| $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$ | pink |
| $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ | green |
| $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ | very pale pink |
| $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ | purple |
| $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ | orange |

With aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ gives a pale blue precipitate, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ a green precipitate that darkens on standing in air as it is oxidised, and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ a red-brown precipitate:

$$\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe(OH)_3(s)}$$

None of these three hydroxides dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how a d-block element or its ion speeds up an industrial or laboratory reaction.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Heterogeneous catalysis** (catalyst in a different phase): iron in the Haber process, $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}$; vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process, $\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3}$; nickel in the hydrogenation of alkenes. Reactant molecules are adsorbed on the metal surface, weakened bonds break more easily, and products leave.

**Homogeneous catalysis** (same phase): $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ions catalyse the slow reaction between iodide and peroxodisulfate ions by switching between +2 and +3:

$$\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$$

$$2\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 2\mathrm{I^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{I_2}$$

The uncatalysed reaction needs two negative ions to collide, and they repel each other. In each catalysed step the colliding ions have opposite charges, so the activation energy is lower, and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is regenerated at the end.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Definition.** A *transition element* is a d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a **partially filled d subshell**. Scandium ($\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is $3d^{0}$) and zinc ($\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is $3d^{10}$) are d-block elements but are **not** transition elements.

**Electronic configurations of the first series** (argon core $[\mathrm{Ar}] = 1s^22s^22p^63s^23p^6$):

| Element | Atomic number | Configuration of the atom |
|---|---|---|
| Sc | 21 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{1}4s^{2}$ |
| Ti | 22 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{2}4s^{2}$ |
| V | 23 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{3}4s^{2}$ |
| Cr | 24 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}4s^{1}$ |
| Mn | 25 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}4s^{2}$ |
| Fe | 26 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{6}4s^{2}$ |
| Co | 27 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{7}4s^{2}$ |
| Ni | 28 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{8}4s^{2}$ |
| Cu | 29 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^{1}$ |
| Zn | 30 | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^{2}$ |

Chromium and copper are exceptions, because a half-filled ($3d^{5}$) or completely filled ($3d^{10}$) subshell is specially stable. When atoms form positive ions, the **4s electrons are lost first**, then the 3d electrons. So $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{6}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}$.

**Characteristic properties** (all arise from the partly filled d subshell):

1. **Variable oxidation states.** The 3d and 4s subshells are close in energy, so electrons from both can be used in bonding and successive ionisation energies rise only gradually. From Ti to Mn the highest oxidation number equals the total number of 4s and 3d electrons (Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7). Iron commonly shows +2 and +3, copper +1 and +2.
2. **Coloured compounds.** In a complex ion the ligands split the five 3d orbitals into two groups separated by a small energy gap $\Delta E$. An electron absorbs a photon of visible light whose energy matches the gap ($\Delta E = h\nu$) and is promoted to the higher group (a d-d transition). The light that is transmitted, the complementary colour of the light absorbed, is the colour we see. Ions with $3d^{0}$ or $3d^{10}$ (for example $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$, $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Cu^{+}}$) have no d-d transition, so their compounds are colourless or white.
3. **Complex formation.** Small, highly charged ions with vacant low-energy orbitals accept lone pairs from ligands to form dative bonds.
4. **Catalytic activity.** Variable oxidation states give alternative reaction routes, and partly filled d orbitals allow reactants to be adsorbed on a metal surface.
5. **Paramagnetism.** Unpaired d electrons make the ions attracted into a magnetic field.

etapes.action: Find the oxidation number of Cr from the overall charge.
etapes.justification: The oxidation numbers of the central ion and ligands add up to the charge on the complex. en is neutral and each chloride is $-1$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $x + 2(0) + 2(-1) = +1$, so $x = +3$. The oxidation number of chromium is **+3**.

etapes.action: Count the dative bonds to chromium.
etapes.justification: The coordination number is the number of dative bonds, and each en forms two.

etapes.action: Write the configuration of the chromium atom, then remove electrons.
etapes.justification: Chromium is an exception: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}4s^{1}$. The 4s electron is lost first, then two 3d electrons.

etapes.action: Place the three 3d electrons in the five 3d orbitals.
etapes.justification: By Hund's rule electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three orbitals each hold one electron: **3 unpaired electrons**.

etapes.justification: Colour needs a partly filled d subshell and ligand-split d orbitals so that a d-d transition can absorb visible light.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $3d^{3}$ is partly filled, so a visible photon can promote an electron between the split d levels and the complex is **coloured**.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The complex ion $[\mathrm{Cr(en)_2Cl_2}]^{+}$ contains chromium (atomic number 24), two molecules of ethane-1,2-diamine (en, a neutral ligand that forms two dative bonds) and two chloride ions.

(a) Determine the oxidation number of chromium.
(b) State the coordination number of chromium.
(c) Write the electronic configuration of the chromium ion in the complex.
(d) State the number of unpaired electrons in this ion.
(e) Explain whether you expect the complex to be coloured.
sections.conclusion_markdown: The chromium ion is $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ with oxidation number +3, coordination number 6, configuration $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{3}$, three unpaired electrons, and the complex is coloured.

items.pourquoi_faux: Electrons are removed from the 4s subshell before the 3d subshell, even though 4s fills first in the atom, because once 3d is occupied it is the lower-energy subshell.
items.correction_markdown: Iron atom: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{6}4s^{2}$. Remove the two 4s electrons: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{6}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: A transition element must form at least one ion with a partly filled d subshell. $\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is $3d^{0}$ and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is $3d^{10}$ and they show no typical transition properties.
items.erreur_markdown: Saying that scandium and zinc are transition elements because they are in the d-block.
items.correction_markdown: Quote the definition: d-block element forming an ion with a partially filled d subshell. Sc and Zn are d-block but not transition elements.

items.pourquoi_faux: A solution shows the light it transmits. It absorbs the complementary colour (red-orange region) and transmits the rest, which we see as blue.
items.erreur_markdown: Saying that a copper(II) solution is blue because the ion absorbs blue light.
items.correction_markdown: State that d-d transitions absorb some wavelengths of visible light and the colour seen is the complementary colour of the light absorbed.

items.pourquoi_faux: The coordination number counts dative bonds to the central ion. Each en is bidentate.
items.erreur_markdown: Giving the coordination number of $[\mathrm{Cu(en)_2}]^{2+}$ as 2 because it has two ligands.
items.correction_markdown: $2 \times 2 = 4$ dative bonds, so the coordination number is **4**.

items.pourquoi_faux: Half-filled and completely filled 3d subshells are especially stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d in chromium and copper.
items.erreur_markdown: Giving the configuration of chromium as $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{4}4s^{2}$ and of copper as $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{9}4s^{2}$.

items.enonce_markdown:
Manganese has atomic number 25 and vanadium has atomic number 23.

(a) Write the electronic configuration of a manganese atom and of the $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ion.
(b) State the number of unpaired electrons in $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$.
(c) Write the configuration of $\mathrm{V^{3+}}$ and state its number of unpaired electrons.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Mn (Z = 25): $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}4s^{2}$. For $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ remove the two 4s electrons: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}$.

(b) The five 3d electrons of $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ occupy five separate orbitals: **5 unpaired electrons**.

(c) V (Z = 23): $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{3}4s^{2}$. For $\mathrm{V^{3+}}$ remove both 4s electrons and one 3d electron: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{2}$. The two 3d electrons are in separate orbitals: **2 unpaired electrons**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The tris(oxalato)ferrate ion is $[\mathrm{Fe(C_2O_4)_3}]^{3-}$. The oxalate ion, $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$, is a bidentate ligand. Iron has atomic number 26.

(a) Determine the oxidation number of iron.
(b) State the coordination number of iron.
(c) Write the electronic configuration of the iron ion.
(d) Would you expect a solution of this complex to be coloured? Give a reason.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $x + 3(-2) = -3$, so $x = +3$. The oxidation number of iron is **+3**.

(b) Each oxalate forms two dative bonds: $3 \times 2 = $ **6**.

(c) Fe: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{6}4s^{2}$. Remove two 4s electrons and one 3d electron: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}$.

(d) Yes. The ion has a partly filled d subshell, so d-d transitions can absorb visible light and the transmitted light is coloured.

items.enonce_markdown:
A sample of iron(II) sulfate crystals was dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. A $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ portion of this solution required $22.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of potassium manganate(VII) solution of concentration $0.0200\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ to reach the end point. The reaction is

$$\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$$

(a) State the change in oxidation number of manganese and of iron.
(b) Explain why no indicator is added.
(c) Calculate the concentration of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ in the solution.
(d) Calculate the mass of iron present in the $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ solution. ($A_r$ of Fe = 55.8)
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Manganese: +7 to +2 (reduced, gains 5 electrons). Iron: +2 to +3 (oxidised, loses 1 electron each).

(b) The manganate(VII) ion is purple and its product $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is almost colourless, so the first permanent pale pink colour shows the end point. The reagent acts as its own indicator.

(c) $n(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}) = 0.0225 \times 0.0200 = 4.50 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}$.
$n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}) = 5 \times 4.50 \times 10^{-4} = 2.25 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ in $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
$[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}] = 2.25 \times 10^{-3} / 0.0250 = $ **$0.0900\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$**.

(d) $n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}})$ in $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ $= 0.0900 \times 0.250 = 0.0225\ \mathrm{mol}$.
Mass $= 0.0225 \times 55.8 = $ **$1.26\ \mathrm{g}$**.

items_markdown: A transition element forms at least one ion with a partially filled d subshell, so Sc and Zn are d-block but not transition elements.
In atoms Cr is 3d5 4s1 and Cu is 3d10 4s1; in positive ions the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons.
Variable oxidation states arise because 3d and 4s are close in energy; the highest oxidation number from Ti to Mn equals the 4s plus 3d electron count.
Colour comes from d-d transitions between ligand-split d orbitals; the colour seen is complementary to the light absorbed, and d0 and d10 ions are colourless.
Coordination number counts dative bonds, not ligands; the metal oxidation number is the complex charge minus the ligand charges.
Catalytic action uses variable oxidation states (homogeneous, for example Fe2+/Fe3+) or surface adsorption (heterogeneous, for example Fe, V2O5, Ni).
